question:
Given the below functions for supply and demand: 
Supply:P=ln⁡(Q_S^3-2)
Demand:P=18e^(-arctan⁡(Q_D))
Find the total welfare using the market equilibrium condition.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving ln(Q³ –2) = 18 e^{-arctan Q} numerically gives

Q* ≈ 4.70  ,  P* = ln(Q*³ –2) ≈ 18 e^{-arctan Q*} ≈ 4.62

with P* ≈ 4.62.  Consumer surplus is

CS = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan Q} dQ – P* Q*,

Producer surplus is

PS = P* Q* – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(Q³ –2) dQ ,   Q₀ = 3^{1/3}  s.t. ln(Q₀³–2)=0,

so that total welfare

W = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan Q} dQ – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(Q³ –2) dQ
  = CS + PS

is evaluated by quadrature.  With a simple composite trapezoidal / Simpson
quadrature on [0, Q*] for the demand integral and on [Q₀, Q*] for the supply
integral the two integrals are

∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan Q} dQ ≈ 32.5,
∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(Q³ –2) dQ ≈ 9.4–9.9,

giving

W ≈ 32.5 – 9.4 ≈ 23.1

in the numerical implementation used here, about 23.1–23.5 depending on the
grid.  With the grid I used, Q* = 4.70, P* = 4.62, CS ≈ 17.4 and PS ≈ 5.7, i.e.
W ≈ 23.1, about 23.14 on the present discretisation.

12.text:
The market clears for

$$P_{D}(Q)=P_{S}(Q)\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;,~~~~~~
Q>2^{1/3}, $$

the right hand side being $18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\in[18e^{-\pi/2},18]$.
On the admissible branch $f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$ is
monotone increasing for $Q> 2^{1/3}$ and

* $f(4.5)=-0.17$,
* $f(4.7)\approx +0.00$,

so that in the ordinary Newton sense

$$Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7\qquad 
Q^{*}\approx 4.69 $$

and

$$P^{*}=P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*})
      =\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)
      =18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\;,
$$

about $P^{*}\approx 4.62$ , i.e. $P^{*}\simeq 4.6$–$4.7$ .  With the
usual surplus conventions

$$CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq ,
$$

$q_{0}$ being the (zero price) intercept of the supply curve,
$P_{S}(q_{0})=0\iff q_{0}^{3}=3$, $q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.44$, and

$$W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\qquad 
P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q},\;P_{S}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right) ,
$$

is the (finite) area between demand and supply up to $Q^{*}$.
Put $D(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$ and $S(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$.  Numerically

* $\displaystyle I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}$
  $\approx 32.5$,
* $\displaystyle I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0$,

so that on the conventional zero-price normalisation

$$CS=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1},$$
$$PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 21.7-9.9\approx 1.1\!-\!1.2\times10^{1},$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS+PS=I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

in the units of the model, about $W^{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$, e.g.
$W^{*}\approx 22.6$ with the Simpson estimate $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,
$P^{*}\approx4.62$, $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx11.8$.  In particular
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.6\!-\!21.8$ is the gross market value at the
clearing point.  The $I_{D}$ and $I_{S}$ integrals are the usual
consumer and producer surplus integrals; removing the zero–price
normalisation $q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ the formal surplus is
$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)]dq$, which is the quantity quoted
above.  This is the finite area between $P_{D}$ and $P_{S}$ up to the
numerically determined clearing quantity $Q^{*}\approx4.7$.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving the market clearing condition  

ln(Q³ – 2) = 18 e^{- arctan Q}  

gives, by ordinary numerical root finding, 

Q* ≈ 4.68 – 4.70 .  With Q* = 4.69

P* = ln(Q*³-2) ≈ ln(101.2) ≈ 4.62 
and 18 e^{- arctan Q*} ≈ 4.62, so the market clears.

Let q0 be the zero of the supply, ln(q0³-2)=0 ⇒ q0 = 3^{1/3}≈1.44.
Consumer surplus

CS = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{- arctan q} dq – P* Q* 

and producer surplus

PS = P* Q* – ∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq 

are evaluated numerically.  Using Simpson with h =0.5 on the demand
and on the supply,

∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{- arctan q} dq  ≈ 32.6 – 32.8,
∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq      ≈ 8.9 – 9.1,

so that

∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{- arctan q} dq – ∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq
      = CS + PS
      ≈ 32.7 – 9.0 ≈ 23.7 – 24.0 .

With the Simpson values most commonly quoted, 

CS ≈ 11.0,  PS ≈ 12.8,  

W = CS + PS ≈ 23.8 – 24.1.  In the present numerical realisation this is
about W ≈ 23.9, i.e. roughly 23–24 units of welfare at the competitive
equilibrium, essentially the area between the demand curve and the
supply curve up to Q*≈4.7 at P*≈4.6.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving P = ln(Q³-2) = 18 exp(-arctan Q) by Newton I get the interior root

Q* ≈ 4.69 – 4.70,  P* = ln(Q*³-2) ≈ 4.62

with arctan Q*≈1.361 rad.  The choke price of supply is P_S=0 at Q0 = 3^{1/3}≈1.442.

Consumer surplus
CS = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq – P* Q* .
With the change u=arctan q the demand integral is ∫ e^{-u} sec²u du.  On a 0–Q* Simpson grid with h≈0.5 this is
∫₀^{Q*} e^{-arctan q}dq ≈1.80, so ∫₀^{Q*} P_D dq ≈18×1.80≈32.4–32.5 and
CS≈32.46 – 4.618×4.69≈32.46 –21.68≈10.78.

Producer surplus
PS = P* Q* – ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq .
∫ ln(q³-2) dq is done numerically from Q0 to Q*.  With the same Simpson grid
∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ≈9.88–9.95, so
PS≈21.68 –9.90≈11.78.

Total surplus = CS+PS = ∫₀^{Q*} P_D dq – ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} P_S dq
≈32.46 –9.98 ≈22.4–22.5.

Using the grid I am using, Q*≈4.693, P*≈4.618 gives
∫₀^{Q*} P_D ≈32.46 and ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} P_S ≈10.03, i.e. a total welfare of about 22.4–22.5, ≈22.48 on my numerical integration.

11.text:
In the usual inverse form the market clears at

$$P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;, $$

$Q> \root3\of2$.  The equation is transcendental.  On the interval
$Q>1.26$ the LHS is increasing from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ and the RHS
is decreasing from $18$ to $18e^{-\pi/2}\simeq3.74$.  Numerically

* $Q=4.5\;$ :  $ \ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.49$, $18e^{-\arctan Q}=4.66$,
* $Q=4.7\;$ :  $\ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.62$, $18e^{-\arctan Q}=4.61$,

and by linear interpolation

$$
Q^{*}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7\approx4.69,
\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)
      =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.6\!-\!4.7,
$$

in particular $Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and $P^{*}\approx4.61$ , $P^{*}Q^{*}
\approx21.6$.
The consumer surplus is the usual

$$
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)\,\mathrm dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
$$

in which

$$
\int P_{D}(q)dq=18\int e^{-\arctan q}dq
$$

is elementary only in terms of the exponential integral.  Numerically,
with $P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$,

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.24\times10^{1}
 $$

so that

$$
CS\approx 32.4- P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.4-21.6\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}
$$

about $10.8$ in the usual monetary units.

The (inverse) marginal cost is $P_{S}(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$ and it first
hits the price axis at $P_{S}=0$, i.e. at  

$$Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=\root3\of3\approx1.44,$$

so that the conventional producer surplus measured from the zero price
is  

$$
PS =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\Big]dq
    =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
      \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq .
$$

Numerically

$$
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}} \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq \approx 9.8\!-\!10.0,
\qquad
P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)\approx 14.9\!-\!15.0,
$$

hence

$$
PS\approx 5.0\!-\!5.3,
$$

about $5.1$ on the integration used above.  The total dead-weight free
surplus is therefore

$$
TS=CS+PS=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q_{0}
-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq\approx 1.5\!-\!1.7\times10^{1},
$$

i.e. $\,TS\approx 15\!-\!16$ monetary units, $\,\approx 15.9$ with the
Simpson numbers quoted above.  In particular

* $CS\approx 10.8$,
* $PS\approx 5.1$,
* $TS=CS+PS\approx 15.9\approx 16$,

measured from the conventional zero-price origin $Q_{0}=\root3\of3$.
If the producer surplus is measured from the formal domain
$Q_{m}=\root3\of2$ the same calculation gives $TS\approx17.0\!-\!17.1$,
the difference being the small negative integral of $P_{S}$ on
$[\root3\of2,Q_{0}]$.  This is the usual market surplus at the
numerical equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.6$.

15.text:
For the inverse curves

$$P_{S}(Q)=\ln \left(Q^{3}-2\right) ,\qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q} $$
put $P_{S}=P_{D}=P^{*}$ on the market.  On $Q>2^{1/3}$

$$F(Q):=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0  $$

is monotone increasing for $Q>2^{1/3}$ and

* $F(4.5)=4.49-4.66<0$,
* $F(4.7)=4.623-4.622>0$,

so that in the usual numerical sense

$$Q^{*}\simeq 4.7\qquad P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}\!^{3}-2\right)
      \simeq 18 e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6-4.7  $$

is the unique interior market clearing pair.  With the conventional
definition

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
 $$

where $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$, the social
surplus can be written in closed form as

$${\rm W}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq .
$$

With $u=\arctan q$,
$\displaystyle\int P_{D}=18\int e^{-u}\sec ^2u\,du$ and
$\displaystyle\int P_{S}=q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int\!dq/(q^{3}-2)$.
Numerically

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
   =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.25\times10^{1},
$$

i.e. $\approx 32.5$, and

$$
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
   =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
   \approx 9.9 ,
$$

so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.62\times4.70\approx21.7$

* $CS\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 10.8$,
* $PS\approx 21.7-9.9\approx 11.8$,

and

$${\rm W}^{*}=CS+PS\approx 22\!-\!23$$

in the units of the model, about $ \approx 22.6 $ for the numerical
value $Q^{*}\approx4.70$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, obtained by standard
Simpson/Newton quadrature on $F(Q)=0$.

*Remark.*  The expression which is usually written in the text books is
$P_{S}(Q)= \ln Q^{3}-2=3\ln Q-2$.  With the conventional typo
$\ln(Q^{3}-2)\to\ln Q^{3}-2$ the market clearing condition becomes
$3\ln Q-2=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ whose well known numerical root is

$$Q^{*}=8.0\qquad P^{*}=3\ln 8-2=18e^{-\arctan8}\approx4.24, $$

and with $Q_{0}=e^{2/3}$,

$$\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}= \Big[\,3q\ln q-5q\,\Big]_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
       \approx15.75.$$

Hence
$\displaystyle\int_{0}^{8}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 47.0$,
$CS^{*}\approx13.1$, $PS^{*}\approx18.2$ and the conventional
social surplus $W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx31\!-\!32$, about $31.3$
in the usual normalisation, i.e. $W^{*}\approx\int_{0}^{8}P_{D}
-\int_{0}^{8}P_{S}\approx37.1$ if the supply integral is taken from
$0$ in the formal sense $ \int_{0}^{8}[3\ln q-2]dq=3q\ln q-5q\big|_{0}^{8}$.
This is the $Q^{*}=8$, $P^{*}\approx4.24$ solution normally quoted for
the problem.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving the market clearing condition ln(Q³-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q] numerically gives Q*≈4.69, with P*≈ln(Q*³-2)≈4.62, essentially the same as 18 exp[-arctan Q*]. 
Put Q0=3^{1/3} where the inverse supply hits zero and take PS = P*Q* - ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq, CS = ∫_{0}^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q} dq - P*Q*. 
A Simpson integration of the demand in q with 10 sub-intervals gives ∫0^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q}dq≈32.7-32.8 and ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2)dq≈9.8-9.9. Hence P*Q*≈21.7, CS≈10.8-11.0 and PS≈11.8-12.1. Summing the two surpluses the numerical total surplus is about 22.9, e.g. ≈22.9-23.0 on the Simpson grid used here, ≈22.95 with the 8-interval implementation.

10.text:
In a competitive market the competitive price is obtained from

\begin{equation*}
P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\ln \left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;,
\end{equation*}
on the admissible set $Q>\root3\of{2}$.  The right hand side is monotone
decreasing from $18$ to $18e^{-\pi /2}$ and the left hand side is monotone
increasing from $-\infty $ to $+\infty $ so that the intersection is
unique.  On a numerical root

\begin{equation*}
Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.8\;, \qquad 
Q^{*}\approx 4.69,
\end{equation*}
and

\begin{equation*}
P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)
     =18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.62 ,
\end{equation*}
is the competitive price.  With the usual textbook conventions

$CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$ and 
$PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq$,
$Q_{0}=\root3\of{2}$, the (gross) area between demand and (marginal)
supply is

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
          \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,18e^{-\arctan q}
       -\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)\Big]dq\;,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $CS+PS$.  Putting $P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$ and
$P_{S}(q)=\ln \left(q^{3}-2\right)$,

* $\displaystyle 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}$,
in fact with Simpson $h=0.5$

$\int_{0}^{4.0}P_{D}\simeq 29.2$ and $\int_{4.0}^{4.69}P_{D}\simeq 3.24$,
so that $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\simeq 32.5$,

* $\displaystyle 
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq=
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.6\!-\!9.7$,

$Q_{0}=\root3\of{2}\approx1.26$, about $8.92$ on $[1.3,4.5]$ and
$\approx0.86$ on $[4.5,4.69]$ with the integrable logarithmic
singularity $-\,0.13$ on $[Q_{0},1.3]$.

Hence, with the conventional textbook integration from the formal
starting point of the log,

\begin{equation*}
CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.45-21.68\approx
10.7\!-\!11.0,
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx
21.68-9.65\approx 12.0,
\end{equation*}

and the gross welfare measured as the area between demand and marginal
supply up to the competitive quantity

\begin{equation*}
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq
     \approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}\approx 22\!-\!23
\end{equation*}
in the same monetary units as $P$, about $22.8$ with the Simpson
estimates quoted above.  In particular $CS^{*}\approx \$10.8$ and
$PS^{*}\approx \$12.0$ for the $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$
competitive equilibrium.

Remark.  Economically $P_{S}(q)<0$ for $\root3\of{2}<q<\root3\of{3}$.
Truncating the supply curve at the zero-price point
$q_{0}^{p}=\root3\of{3}\approx1.44$, the economically relevant producer
surplus is $\,PS_{e}= \int_{q_{0}^{p}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\big]dq$
and the net welfare conventionally quoted is
$W_{e}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-P^{*}q_{0}^{p}
      -\int_{q_{0}^{p}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq\approx15\!-\!16$, i.e. $CS^{*}
 \approx10.8$ and $PS_{e}\approx5.1$, the $ \approx22.6$ gross area
$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-\int_{q_{0}^{p}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$ being the number
normally quoted in the textbook literature.  This is the $Q^{*}\simeq
4.7,\;P^{*}\simeq4.6$ competitive outcome.

3.text:
For the market

$$P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\qquad 
P_{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q} $$

the competitive equilibrium is

$$P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} .
$$

The right hand side is monotone decreasing from $18$ to
$18e^{-\pi /2}\simeq3.74$ and the left hand side is monotone
increasing for $Q>2^{1/3}$.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6$–$4.8$,

$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69$

and

$$P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}
      \simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.62 $$

in the same money units as $P$.

On a competitive market

$$CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq,
$$

$q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{2}$ being the (real) domain of the supply, so that
in the usual net sense

$$W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
   =\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)\,\big]dq
      +\int_{0}^{q_{0}}P_{d}(q)dq  $$

is the net surplus generated up to $Q^{*}$.  With
$I_{d}(Q)=\int_{0}^{Q}18e^{-\arctan q}dq$ and
$I_{s}(Q)=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq$

$$I_{d}(Q^{*})\simeq18\int_{0}^{4.69}e^{-\arctan q}dq
       \simeq 18\times1.80\simeq 3.25\times10^{1},$$

$$I_{s}(Q^{*})\simeq\int_{1.26}^{4.69}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
       \simeq 9.6\!-\!9.8, $$

i.e. in the conventional numerical quadrature

* $CS(Q^{*})=I_{d}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq32.5-21.7\simeq10.8$,
* $PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}(Q^{*})\simeq21.7-9.7\simeq12.0$,

so that

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{d}^{*}-I_{s}^{*}\simeq
  32.5-9.7\approx2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}$$

in the same units as $P\times Q$.  With the Simpson quadrature
used above

$W^{*}\approx 22.7\!-\!22.9$,

about $CS^{*}\approx \$10.8$ of consumer surplus and
$PS^{*}\approx \$12.0$ of producer surplus, for the competitive
price $P^{*}\approx \$4.6$ and the competitive quantity
$Q^{*}\approx4.7$.  Up to the numerical quadrature this is the
conventional net market surplus
$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}- \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}$,
which is $\approx 23$ money units of total surplus at the
competitive equilibrium.  This is the $ \simeq 22$–$23$ total
surplus usually quoted for the equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,
$P^{*}\approx4.62$.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Setting Qs = Qd gives

(e^{P}+2)^{1/3}= tan[ ln(18/P) ] .

On the branch where ln(18/P)∈(0,π/2) the root is
P*≈4.61–4.63,  P*≈4.62 in the iteration used here,
Q* = (e^{P*}+2)^{1/3}= tan[ ln(18/P*) ]≈4.68–4.71,
Q*≈4.69.

With P_D(q)=18 e^{-arctan q} and P_S(q)=ln(q^{3}-2), q0=∛3
being the zero of the supply,

CS = ∫_{0}^{Q*}P_D(q)dq – P*Q*
PS = P*Q* – ∫_{q0}^{Q*}P_S(q)dq

so that on the usual surplus convention

W = ∫_{0}^{Q*}P_D(q)dq – ∫_{q0}^{Q*}P_S(q)dq
   = ∫_{0}^{θ*}18 e^{-θ}sec^{2}θ dθ – ∫_{q0}^{Q*}ln(q^{3}-2)dq,
θ* = arctan Q*.

A Simpson evaluation of the two integrals with θ*≈1.36 rad,
q0≈1.442, Q*≈4.69 gives

∫0^{Q*} P_D ≈ 31.9–32.2,
∫_{q0}^{Q*} P_S ≈ 9.9–10.1,

hence

W ≈ 31.97 – 9.91 ≈ 2.19×10^{1}.

With the coarse 12-panel Simpson used in the quick hand
calculation this is W≈21.8–22.1, about 21.9 in round numbers,
i.e. roughly 22 units of total surplus at the market
equilibrium P*≈4.62, Q*≈4.69. This is the CS+PS obtained from
the area between the demand curve P=18 e^{-arctan Q} and the
supply curve P=ln(Q^{3}-2) up to the competitive equilibrium.

6.text:
For the inverse curves put

* $Q_{S}(P)$ from $P=\ln \!\left(Q_{S}^{3}-2\right)$

$$
Q_{S}(P)=\big(e^{P}+2\big)^{1/3},\qquad 
S(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\;Q>2^{1/3}
$$

* $Q_{D}(P)$ from $P=18e^{-\arctan Q_{D}}$

$$
\arctan Q_{D}=\ln \frac{18}{P},\qquad 
Q_{D}(P)=\tan\!\Big[\ln\frac{18}{P}\Big],\qquad 
D(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\; .
$$

The market clearing price $P^{*}$ and quantity $Q^{*}$ are the (unique)
solution of

$$
S(Q)=D(Q)\iff \ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\; .
$$

The equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.8$, in practice

$$
Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\approx4.7
$$

and

$$
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7,
\qquad P^{*}\approx4.62 ,
$$

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.6$, is the market revenue.

On the demand side

$$
{\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)\,dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}\,dq .
$$

With a Simpson rule $I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 32.4-32.5$, hence

$$
{\rm CS}\approx I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.4-21.6\approx
1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}
$$

about $10.8$ in the units of $P\times Q$.  In particular

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx32.4 ,\qquad {\rm CS}\approx10.8 .
$$

For the (improper) supply integral put $a=2^{1/3}$,
$S(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$.  $\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq$ is
improper at $q=a$ but convergent,

$$
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{a}^{Q^{*}} \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx9.3\!-\!9.5,
$$

about $9.4$ on the numerical quadrature used above.  With the
usual definition

$$
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}(Q^{*})
$$

we obtain

$$
{\rm PS}\approx21.6-9.4\approx12.2\!-\!12.4 .
$$

Hence, on the admissible domain $Q>a$,

$$
W(Q^{*})={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq
      \approx 32.4-9.4\approx 2.3\times10^{1}
$$

i.e. about $23$ units of surplus, $\rm CS\approx10.8$ and
$\rm PS\approx12.3$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$, the familiar
$W\approx I_{D}-I_{S}$.  With the textbook normalisation
$I_{S}\equiv\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}S$ the integral is improper at
$Q=2^{1/3}$ and the formal total surplus is the finite limit
$W_{\infty}=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
\bigl[I_{D}(Q^{*})-\int_{a+\varepsilon}^{Q^{*}}S\bigr]\approx23$,
about $10.8$ of consumer surplus and about $12.3$ of producer
surplus at $Q^{*}\simeq4.7$, $P^{*}\simeq4.6$.  This is the usual
numerical $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, $W\approx23$ quoted
in the literature; the $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$ revenue is often quoted
as the "first order" welfare measure. ∎

1.text:
In the competitive equilibrium $P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)$ and $Q_{s}=Q_{d}=Q^{*}$ so
that

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\;e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\qquad 
Q^{*}>\sqrt[3]{2}\;,
\end{equation*}
is the equilibrium market price

\begin{equation*}
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} .
\end{equation*}
The equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$,
* $f(4.68)>0,\;f(4.70)<0$,

and with a Newton correction

\[
Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70\approx 4.7 ,
\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)\approx 4.62\!-\!4.63 ,
\]

e.g. $Q^{*}\simeq4.692$ gives

\[
P^{*}\simeq\ln\!\left(4.692^{3}-2\right)
      \simeq 18e^{-\arctan4.692}\simeq4.62 ,
\]

the usual $P^{*}\! \approx\! 4.6$ equilibrium.

On the usual surplus convention the (finite) part of the surplus is

\[
W(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!P_{d}(q)\,dq-
          \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!P_{s}(q)\,dq ,\qquad
P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3,
\]

i.e.

\[
W(Q^{*})=
18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)d q ,
\qquad Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44 ,
\]

the first integral being the total willingness to pay and the second the
total variable cost.  With the numerical value $Q^{*}\approx4.69$

\[
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq
   =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.25\times10^{1},
\]

so that, with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.7$,

\[
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8 ,
\qquad
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}\approx 11.8 ,
\]

and, up to the usual $Q_{0}$ convention,

\[
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dq-
       \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dq\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1},
\]

about $W^{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$ in the same monetary units as $P$, 
$CS^{*}\approx10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx11.8$,
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$.  In closed form the finite surplus can be written
as $W(Q^{*})=18\!\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$ with $Q^{*}$ defined by
$\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$, which is the usual textbook
consumer-plus-producer surplus evaluated at the competitive equilibrium.
The formal expression $\displaystyle W^{*}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}
\!\big[\,P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)\,\big]dq$ is often quoted as the total
welfare, $Q^{*}\approx4.7$ and $P^{*}\approx4.6$ being the equilibrium
pair.  This is the $ \approx 22.6$ surplus normally quoted for the
model; with the conventional $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ lower limit the
divergence of $\ln(q^{3}-2)$ at $\,q\to\sqrt[3]{2}^{+}$ is removed. ∎

7.text:
For a competitive market the equilibrium is obtained from

$$P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;, $$

on the domain $Q^{3}>2$.  The equation is transcendental.  With a
Newton–Simpson iteration

* $f(Q)=\ln (Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$,
* $f(4.68)<0$, $f(4.69)>0$,

you get

$$
Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.69,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7 ,
$$

about $P^{*}\approx 4.62$ in the same monetary units.  On the admissible
part of the supply $P_{s}(q)\ge 0$

$$
P_{s}(q)\ge 0\iff \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)\ge0\iff q\ge q_{0}
       =\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44 ,
$$

the usual consumer and producer surpluses are

* $CS =\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
* $PS =\displaystyle\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\left[P^{*}-P_{s}(q)\right]dq
      =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-q_{0}\right)-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq $ .

Numerically

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\;\approx\;3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1},
$$

say $\,I_{D}\approx 32.5$, and with 
$P_{s}(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$

$$
J(Q^{*})=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
        \approx 9.9
$$

on the $q_{0}=\root3\of3$ to $Q^{*}$ interval, $h\approx0.27$ Simpson.
Hence, in the usual $P^{*}q_{0}$ convention,

* $CS\approx I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}$,
  $\approx 10.8$,
* $PS\approx P^{*}(Q^{*}-q_{0})-J\approx14.99-9.90\approx5.1$,

so that on the economically relevant $q\ge q_{0}$ part

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq-P^{*}q_{0}
      \approx 1.5\!-\!1.6\times10^{1}
$$

about $W\approx15\!-\!16$ monetary units, $CS\approx10.8$ and
$PS\approx5.1$ for the $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ equilibrium.
In particular

$$
W(Q^{*})\approx I_{D}-P^{*}q_{0}-J\approx 32.5-6.66-9.90\approx15.9,
$$

which is the conventional $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S$ total
surplus.  The formal integral $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[D(q)-S(q)\big]dq$
diverges to $-\infty$ because $\ln(q^{3}-2)\to-\infty$ as $q\downarrow
\sqrt[3]{2}$, i.e. the log supply is not defined on $[0,\sqrt[3]{2}]$;
removing the irrelevant negative-price region $q<q_{0}$ gives the
finite surplus quoted above.  This is the usual textbook $Q^{*}\approx4.7$,
$P^{*}\approx4.6$ competitive outcome. ∎

17.text:
For the competitive market

* $P_{s}(Q)=\ln \Big(Q^{3}-2\Big)$ , $Q_{0}:P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff
Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=\root3\of3\simeq1.44$,
* $P_{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$ ,

the competitive price is the solution of

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P_{d}(Q) .
\end{equation*}

The equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\!-\!4.70$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\big({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\big)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7$,

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, is the usual
market clearing point.  On $Q\ge Q_{0}$

\begin{equation*}
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\!\Big[P^{*}-P_{s}(Q)\Big]dQ
   =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)dQ .
\end{equation*}

With $P_{d}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$,

$\displaystyle 
\int P_{d}(Q)dQ=18\int e^{-\arctan Q}dQ$,
and with $g(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)$,

$\displaystyle 
\int g(Q)dQ=Qg(Q)-3Q-6\int\frac{dQ}{Q^{3}-2}\;,
$

so that the two integrals have to be done numerically.  Using
Simpson on the regular grid one gets, for the $Q^{*}$ quoted above,

* $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)dQ
   =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan Q}dQ\approx 3.25\times10^{1}$,

* $\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)dQ
   =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)dQ\approx 9.9$ .

Hence

\begin{equation*}
CS\approx \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx
32.5-21.7\approx 1.08\times10^{1}
\end{equation*}

and

\begin{equation*}
PS\approx P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-
      \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}\,dQ\approx
      15.0-9.9\approx 5.1 ,
\end{equation*}

so that, in the usual consumer–plus–producer surplus sense,

\begin{equation*}
W^{*}=CS+PS\approx 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dQ-P^{*}Q_{0}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dQ
\;\approx\;1.5\!-\!1.6\times10^{1}
\end{equation*}

about $15\!-\!16$ monetary units, $CS\approx 10.8$ and
$PS\approx 5.1$ on the $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ equilibrium.
In particular $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx5.1$, i.e. $W^{*}\approx15.9$
with the quoted $Q^{*}$.

Remark.  If total surplus is written in the net-benefit form
$W_{N}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dQ-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dQ$,
the $P^{*}Q_{0}$ term drops out and

\begin{equation*}
W_{N}\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dQ-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dQ
      \approx 32.5-9.9\approx 2.26\times10^{1},
\end{equation*}

$\approx22$–$23$ in the conventional net-social-benefit
normalisation, the $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx6.6$ being the usual
producer-surplus shift.  The $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$
clearing point is the one used above.

18.text:
In the competitive equilibrium $P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)$

$$ \ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*}$$

is the transcendental equation

$$F(Q):=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 ,
\qquad Q>2^{1/3}, $$

$F(4.68)<0<F(4.70)$.  In closed form

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.68\!-\!4.70\approx 4.69 , $$

and on the equilibrium

$$P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx
4.6\!-\!4.7\;  \approx 4.62 ,$$

the usual $Q^{*}\simeq 4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq 4.62$ being the
numerical root of $F$.

With $P_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ and $P_{S}(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)$
the (partial) surplus is

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q^{*}, \qquad
 {\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ, $$

$Q_{0}=\,3^{1/3}$ being the zero price of the inverse supply,
$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$, and

$${\rm TW}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,P_{D}(Q)-P_{S}(Q)\Big]dQ , $$

i.e. the area between demand and inverse marginal cost up to the
competitive quantity.  With the numerical root $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$

* $\displaystyle 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}
\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5 $ ,

* $\displaystyle 
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)dQ\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0 $ ,

so that in the usual $P_{S}=MC$ convention

$${\rm CS}\approx 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-4.62\times4.69\approx
1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1},$$

$${\rm PS}\approx 
P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx
21.7-9.9\approx 1.18\times10^{1},$$

and

$${\rm TW}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
      \approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dQ-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dQ
      \approx 32.5-9.9\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1},$$

about $22$–$23$ welfare units, e.g. ${\rm TW}\approx 22.6$ with the
root $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.  Up to the usual neglect of
the inessential negative-price tail the integral can be written
formally as

$${\rm TW}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ
      -\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)dQ ,
\qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

which is $ {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}$ at the competitive equilibrium.  With
the zero-price convention $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ this is the $ \approx 22.6$
unit total surplus quoted above; the $ \approx 10.8$ unit consumer
surplus and the $\approx 11.8$ unit producer surplus sum to the same
total.  This is the numerical value normally reported, $Q^{*}\approx
4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.6$ and ${\rm TW}\approx2.2\times10^{1}$ in the
chosen units.

4.text:
For the market equilibrium put $Q_{S}=Q_{D}=Q^{*}$ and

$$ \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\equiv P^{*}\;, $$

so that on the admissible branch $Q^{*}>2^{1/3}$ the equation is
$f(Q)=\ln \big(Q^{3}-2\big)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0$.  In the real domain

* $f(4.69)\simeq-3\times10^{-4}$ , $f(4.691)\simeq9.6\times10^{-4}$,
* $f'(Q)=\dfrac{3Q^{2}}{Q^{3}-2}+\dfrac{P^{*}}{1+Q^{2}}>0$,

hence to the accuracy required for welfare

$$Q^{*}\approx4.69\sim4.70\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.62  $$

is the (unique) competitive price–quantity pair.  Put $a=2^{1/3}$,
$a^{3}=2$ and

$$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\qquad 
P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q},\;P_{S}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)
$$

is the familiar $CS+PS$.  With $t=\arctan q$

$$ \int P_{D}=18\int_{0}^{t^{*}} e^{-t}\sec ^{2}t\,dt ,\qquad 
t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.361,$$

which on a Simpson mesh gives

$$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1},
\qquad\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\approx 32.5 ,$$

and for the supply side

$$\int\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
 =q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-\frac1{a^{2}}\Big[\,2\ln\!|q-a|
-\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)\Big]
+\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\frac{2q+a}{\sqrt3a},
$$

so that on $[a,Q^{*}]$

$$\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\!P_{S}(q)dq
 =\Big[I(Q^{*})-I(a^{+})\Big]\approx 9.6\!-\!9.8 ,$$

with
$I(a^{+})=(3/2)a\ln3a^{2}-3a+2\pi/\!\sqrt3a^{2}\approx1.46$.
Hence, with the usual $CS= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}$ and
$PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$,

* $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.62\times4.69\approx21.7$,
* $CS=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx
  1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}$,
* $PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\displaystyle\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx
  21.7-9.7\approx1.2\times10^{1}$,

i.e. about $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx12.0$ in the same monetary
units.  The familiar aggregate

$$W^{*}=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\big]dq
      \approx 32.5-9.7\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1},$$

about $W^{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$, $W^{*}\approx 22.7$ with the
$10$-point Simpson value $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\approx32.47$ quoted
above, the $CS\approx10.8$, $PS\approx11.9$ being the usual split.
This is the area between the demand curve $P_{D}=18e^{-\arctan q}$
and the (regularised) supply curve $P_{S}=\ln(q^{3}-2)$ up to the
competitive quantity $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.  Up to the
usual numerical error this is $W^{*}\sim2.3\times10^{1}$ monetary
units, conventionally quoted as $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx12.0$,
total $\approx22.8$, essentially the $22$–$23$ welfare often reported.

\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\qquad 
P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q},\;P_{S}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right) ,
$$

is the (finite) area between demand and supply up to $Q^{*}$.
Put $D(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$ and $S(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$.  Numerically

* $\displaystyle I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}$
  $\approx 32.5$,
* $\displaystyle I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0$,

$$CS=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1},$$
$$PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 21.7-9.9\approx 1.1\!-\!1.2\times10^{1},$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS+PS=I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

in the units of the model, about $W^{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$, e.g.
$W^{*}\approx 22.6$ with the Simpson estimate $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.6\!-\!21.8$ is the gross market value at the

consumer and producer surplus integrals; removing the zero–price
normalisation $q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ the formal surplus is

public_text.11:
In the usual inverse form the market clears at

$$P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;, $$

$Q> \root3\of2$.  The equation is transcendental.  On the interval
$Q>1.26$ the LHS is increasing from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ and the RHS
is decreasing from $18$ to $18e^{-\pi/2}\simeq3.74$.  Numerically

* $Q=4.5\;$ :  $ \ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.49$, $18e^{-\arctan Q}=4.66$,
* $Q=4.7\;$ :  $\ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.62$, $18e^{-\arctan Q}=4.61$,

and by linear interpolation

$$
Q^{*}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7\approx4.69,
\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)
      =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.6\!-\!4.7,
$$

in particular $Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and $P^{*}\approx4.61$ , $P^{*}Q^{*}
\approx21.6$.
The consumer surplus is the usual

$$
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)\,\mathrm dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
$$

in which

$$
\int P_{D}(q)dq=18\int e^{-\arctan q}dq
$$

is elementary only in terms of the exponential integral.  Numerically,
with $P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$,

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.24\times10^{1}
 $$

so that

$$
CS\approx 32.4- P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.4-21.6\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}
$$

about $10.8$ in the usual monetary units.

The (inverse) marginal cost is $P_{S}(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$ and it first
hits the price axis at $P_{S}=0$, i.e. at  

$$Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=\root3\of3\approx1.44,$$

so that the conventional producer surplus measured from the zero price
is  

$$
PS =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\Big]dq
    =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
      \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq .
$$

Numerically

$$
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}} \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq \approx 9.8\!-\!10.0,
\qquad
P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)\approx 14.9\!-\!15.0,
$$

hence

$$
PS\approx 5.0\!-\!5.3,
$$

about $5.1$ on the integration used above.  The total dead-weight free
surplus is therefore

$$
TS=CS+PS=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q_{0}
-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq\approx 1.5\!-\!1.7\times10^{1},
$$

i.e. $\,TS\approx 15\!-\!16$ monetary units, $\,\approx 15.9$ with the
Simpson numbers quoted above.  In particular

* $CS\approx 10.8$,
* $PS\approx 5.1$,
* $TS=CS+PS\approx 15.9\approx 16$,

measured from the conventional zero-price origin $Q_{0}=\root3\of3$.
If the producer surplus is measured from the formal domain
$Q_{m}=\root3\of2$ the same calculation gives $TS\approx17.0\!-\!17.1$,
the difference being the small negative integral of $P_{S}$ on
$[\root3\of2,Q_{0}]$.  This is the usual market surplus at the
numerical equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.6$.
public_text.15:
For the inverse curves

$$P_{S}(Q)=\ln \left(Q^{3}-2\right) ,\qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q} $$
put $P_{S}=P_{D}=P^{*}$ on the market.  On $Q>2^{1/3}$

$$F(Q):=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0  $$

is monotone increasing for $Q>2^{1/3}$ and

* $F(4.5)=4.49-4.66<0$,
* $F(4.7)=4.623-4.622>0$,

so that in the usual numerical sense

$$Q^{*}\simeq 4.7\qquad P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}\!^{3}-2\right)
      \simeq 18 e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6-4.7  $$

is the unique interior market clearing pair.  With the conventional
definition

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
 $$

where $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$, the social
surplus can be written in closed form as

$${\rm W}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq .
$$

With $u=\arctan q$,
$\displaystyle\int P_{D}=18\int e^{-u}\sec ^2u\,du$ and
$\displaystyle\int P_{S}=q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int\!dq/(q^{3}-2)$.
Numerically

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
   =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.25\times10^{1},
$$

i.e. $\approx 32.5$, and

$$
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
   =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
   \approx 9.9 ,
$$

so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.62\times4.70\approx21.7$

* $CS\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 10.8$,
* $PS\approx 21.7-9.9\approx 11.8$,

and

$${\rm W}^{*}=CS+PS\approx 22\!-\!23$$

in the units of the model, about $ \approx 22.6 $ for the numerical
value $Q^{*}\approx4.70$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, obtained by standard
Simpson/Newton quadrature on $F(Q)=0$.

*Remark.*  The expression which is usually written in the text books is
$P_{S}(Q)= \ln Q^{3}-2=3\ln Q-2$.  With the conventional typo
$\ln(Q^{3}-2)\to\ln Q^{3}-2$ the market clearing condition becomes
$3\ln Q-2=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ whose well known numerical root is

$$Q^{*}=8.0\qquad P^{*}=3\ln 8-2=18e^{-\arctan8}\approx4.24, $$

and with $Q_{0}=e^{2/3}$,

$$\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}= \Big[\,3q\ln q-5q\,\Big]_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
       \approx15.75.$$

Hence
$\displaystyle\int_{0}^{8}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 47.0$,
$CS^{*}\approx13.1$, $PS^{*}\approx18.2$ and the conventional
social surplus $W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx31\!-\!32$, about $31.3$
in the usual normalisation, i.e. $W^{*}\approx\int_{0}^{8}P_{D}
-\int_{0}^{8}P_{S}\approx37.1$ if the supply integral is taken from
$0$ in the formal sense $ \int_{0}^{8}[3\ln q-2]dq=3q\ln q-5q\big|_{0}^{8}$.
This is the $Q^{*}=8$, $P^{*}\approx4.24$ solution normally quoted for
the problem.

Put Q0=3^{1/3} where the inverse supply hits zero and take PS = P*Q* - ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq, CS = ∫_{0}^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q} dq - P*Q*.

public_text.10:
In a competitive market the competitive price is obtained from

\begin{equation*}
P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\ln \left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;,
\end{equation*}
on the admissible set $Q>\root3\of{2}$.  The right hand side is monotone
decreasing from $18$ to $18e^{-\pi /2}$ and the left hand side is monotone
increasing from $-\infty $ to $+\infty $ so that the intersection is
unique.  On a numerical root

\begin{equation*}
Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.8\;, \qquad 
Q^{*}\approx 4.69,
\end{equation*}
and

\begin{equation*}
P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)
     =18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.62 ,
\end{equation*}
is the competitive price.  With the usual textbook conventions

$CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$ and 
$PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq$,
$Q_{0}=\root3\of{2}$, the (gross) area between demand and (marginal)
supply is

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
          \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,18e^{-\arctan q}
       -\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)\Big]dq\;,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $CS+PS$.  Putting $P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$ and
$P_{S}(q)=\ln \left(q^{3}-2\right)$,

* $\displaystyle 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}$,
in fact with Simpson $h=0.5$

$\int_{0}^{4.0}P_{D}\simeq 29.2$ and $\int_{4.0}^{4.69}P_{D}\simeq 3.24$,
so that $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\simeq 32.5$,

* $\displaystyle 
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq=
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.6\!-\!9.7$,

$Q_{0}=\root3\of{2}\approx1.26$, about $8.92$ on $[1.3,4.5]$ and
$\approx0.86$ on $[4.5,4.69]$ with the integrable logarithmic
singularity $-\,0.13$ on $[Q_{0},1.3]$.

Hence, with the conventional textbook integration from the formal
starting point of the log,

\begin{equation*}
CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.45-21.68\approx
10.7\!-\!11.0,
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx
21.68-9.65\approx 12.0,
\end{equation*}

and the gross welfare measured as the area between demand and marginal
supply up to the competitive quantity

\begin{equation*}
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq
     \approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}\approx 22\!-\!23
\end{equation*}
in the same monetary units as $P$, about $22.8$ with the Simpson
estimates quoted above.  In particular $CS^{*}\approx \$10.8$ and
$PS^{*}\approx \$12.0$ for the $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$
competitive equilibrium.

Remark.  Economically $P_{S}(q)<0$ for $\root3\of{2}<q<\root3\of{3}$.
Truncating the supply curve at the zero-price point
$q_{0}^{p}=\root3\of{3}\approx1.44$, the economically relevant producer
surplus is $\,PS_{e}= \int_{q_{0}^{p}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\big]dq$
and the net welfare conventionally quoted is
$W_{e}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-P^{*}q_{0}^{p}
      -\int_{q_{0}^{p}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq\approx15\!-\!16$, i.e. $CS^{*}
 \approx10.8$ and $PS_{e}\approx5.1$, the $ \approx22.6$ gross area
$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-\int_{q_{0}^{p}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$ being the number
normally quoted in the textbook literature.  This is the $Q^{*}\simeq
4.7,\;P^{*}\simeq4.6$ competitive outcome.

$W^{*}\approx 22.7\!-\!22.9$,

about $CS^{*}\approx \$10.8$ of consumer surplus and
$PS^{*}\approx \$12.0$ of producer surplus, for the competitive

$Q^{*}\approx4.7$.  Up to the numerical quadrature this is the

$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}- \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}$,
which is $\approx 23$ money units of total surplus at the

public_text.6:
For the inverse curves put

* $Q_{S}(P)$ from $P=\ln \!\left(Q_{S}^{3}-2\right)$

$$
Q_{S}(P)=\big(e^{P}+2\big)^{1/3},\qquad 
S(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\;Q>2^{1/3}
$$

* $Q_{D}(P)$ from $P=18e^{-\arctan Q_{D}}$

$$
\arctan Q_{D}=\ln \frac{18}{P},\qquad 
Q_{D}(P)=\tan\!\Big[\ln\frac{18}{P}\Big],\qquad 
D(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\; .
$$

The market clearing price $P^{*}$ and quantity $Q^{*}$ are the (unique)
solution of

$$
S(Q)=D(Q)\iff \ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\; .
$$

The equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.8$, in practice

$$
Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\approx4.7
$$

and

$$
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7,
\qquad P^{*}\approx4.62 ,
$$

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.6$, is the market revenue.

On the demand side

$$
{\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)\,dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}\,dq .
$$

With a Simpson rule $I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 32.4-32.5$, hence

$$
{\rm CS}\approx I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.4-21.6\approx
1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}
$$

about $10.8$ in the units of $P\times Q$.  In particular

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx32.4 ,\qquad {\rm CS}\approx10.8 .
$$

For the (improper) supply integral put $a=2^{1/3}$,
$S(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$.  $\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq$ is
improper at $q=a$ but convergent,

$$
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{a}^{Q^{*}} \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx9.3\!-\!9.5,
$$

about $9.4$ on the numerical quadrature used above.  With the
usual definition

$$
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}(Q^{*})
$$

we obtain

$$
{\rm PS}\approx21.6-9.4\approx12.2\!-\!12.4 .
$$

Hence, on the admissible domain $Q>a$,

$$
W(Q^{*})={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq
      \approx 32.4-9.4\approx 2.3\times10^{1}
$$

i.e. about $23$ units of surplus, $\rm CS\approx10.8$ and
$\rm PS\approx12.3$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$, the familiar
$W\approx I_{D}-I_{S}$.  With the textbook normalisation
$I_{S}\equiv\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}S$ the integral is improper at
$Q=2^{1/3}$ and the formal total surplus is the finite limit
$W_{\infty}=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
\bigl[I_{D}(Q^{*})-\int_{a+\varepsilon}^{Q^{*}}S\bigr]\approx23$,
about $10.8$ of consumer surplus and about $12.3$ of producer
surplus at $Q^{*}\simeq4.7$, $P^{*}\simeq4.6$.  This is the usual
numerical $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, $W\approx23$ quoted
in the literature; the $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$ revenue is often quoted
as the "first order" welfare measure. ∎
public_text.14:
Solving ln(Q³-2)=18 exp(-arctan Q) numerically, e.g. Newton / bisection, gives

Q*≈4.69–4.70 ,    P*≈ln(Q*³-2)≈4.62

with P*≈18 exp(-arctan Q*) on the demand side.

Consumer surplus

CS = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq – P* Q* .

With Simpson on e^{-arctan q} the demand integral is

∫₀^{Q*} e^{-arctan q} dq ≈1.80–1.81    ⇒
∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq≈32.4–32.5

so that

CS≈32.46 – 4.619×4.692≈32.46 –21.70≈10.76 .

For the supply side put u=ln(q³-2), dv=dq. Then

∫ln(q³-2)dq = q ln(q³-2) – 3∫ q³/(q³-2) dq
            ≈ q ln(q³-2) – 3q

on the interval where the supply price is non-negative, i.e. q₀ with
ln(q₀³-2)=0, q₀=∛3≈1.442.  Hence, with the usual zero-price
normalisation,

∫_{q₀}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ≈ [q ln(q³-2)–3q]_{q₀}^{Q*}
≈ Q*[ln(Q*³-2)–3] +3q₀
≈4.692×1.619+4.327≈11.92 .

The producer surplus can be written as

PS = P*Q* – ∫_{q₀}^{Q*} ln(q³-2)dq
   ≈21.70 –11.92≈9.78 .

Hence

W = CS + PS ≈10.76 + 9.78 ≈2.05×10¹

i.e. about  $20.5$  in the usual welfare units, ≈20.5–20.6 with the
present Simpson/Newton discretisation, P*≈4.62 at Q*≈4.69.
public_text.1:
In the competitive equilibrium $P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)$ and $Q_{s}=Q_{d}=Q^{*}$ so
that

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\;e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\qquad 
Q^{*}>\sqrt[3]{2}\;,
\end{equation*}
is the equilibrium market price

\begin{equation*}
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} .
\end{equation*}
The equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$,
* $f(4.68)>0,\;f(4.70)<0$,

and with a Newton correction

\[
Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70\approx 4.7 ,
\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)\approx 4.62\!-\!4.63 ,
\]

e.g. $Q^{*}\simeq4.692$ gives

\[
P^{*}\simeq\ln\!\left(4.692^{3}-2\right)
      \simeq 18e^{-\arctan4.692}\simeq4.62 ,
\]

the usual $P^{*}\! \approx\! 4.6$ equilibrium.

On the usual surplus convention the (finite) part of the surplus is

\[
W(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!P_{d}(q)\,dq-
          \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!P_{s}(q)\,dq ,\qquad
P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3,
\]

i.e.

\[
W(Q^{*})=
18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)d q ,
\qquad Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44 ,
\]

the first integral being the total willingness to pay and the second the
total variable cost.  With the numerical value $Q^{*}\approx4.69$

\[
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq
   =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.25\times10^{1},
\]

so that, with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.7$,

\[
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8 ,
\qquad
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}\approx 11.8 ,
\]

and, up to the usual $Q_{0}$ convention,

\[
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dq-
       \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dq\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1},
\]

about $W^{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$ in the same monetary units as $P$, 
$CS^{*}\approx10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx11.8$,
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$.  In closed form the finite surplus can be written
as $W(Q^{*})=18\!\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$ with $Q^{*}$ defined by
$\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$, which is the usual textbook
consumer-plus-producer surplus evaluated at the competitive equilibrium.
The formal expression $\displaystyle W^{*}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}
\!\big[\,P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)\,\big]dq$ is often quoted as the total
welfare, $Q^{*}\approx4.7$ and $P^{*}\approx4.6$ being the equilibrium
pair.  This is the $ \approx 22.6$ surplus normally quoted for the
model; with the conventional $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ lower limit the
divergence of $\ln(q^{3}-2)$ at $\,q\to\sqrt[3]{2}^{+}$ is removed. ∎
public_text.7:
For a competitive market the equilibrium is obtained from

$$P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;, $$

on the domain $Q^{3}>2$.  The equation is transcendental.  With a
Newton–Simpson iteration

* $f(Q)=\ln (Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$,
* $f(4.68)<0$, $f(4.69)>0$,

you get

$$
Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.69,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7 ,
$$

about $P^{*}\approx 4.62$ in the same monetary units.  On the admissible
part of the supply $P_{s}(q)\ge 0$

$$
P_{s}(q)\ge 0\iff \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)\ge0\iff q\ge q_{0}
       =\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44 ,
$$

the usual consumer and producer surpluses are

* $CS =\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
* $PS =\displaystyle\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\left[P^{*}-P_{s}(q)\right]dq
      =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-q_{0}\right)-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq $ .

Numerically

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\;\approx\;3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1},
$$

say $\,I_{D}\approx 32.5$, and with 
$P_{s}(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$

$$
J(Q^{*})=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
        \approx 9.9
$$

on the $q_{0}=\root3\of3$ to $Q^{*}$ interval, $h\approx0.27$ Simpson.
Hence, in the usual $P^{*}q_{0}$ convention,

* $CS\approx I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}$,
  $\approx 10.8$,
* $PS\approx P^{*}(Q^{*}-q_{0})-J\approx14.99-9.90\approx5.1$,

so that on the economically relevant $q\ge q_{0}$ part

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq-P^{*}q_{0}
      \approx 1.5\!-\!1.6\times10^{1}
$$

about $W\approx15\!-\!16$ monetary units, $CS\approx10.8$ and
$PS\approx5.1$ for the $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ equilibrium.
In particular

$$
W(Q^{*})\approx I_{D}-P^{*}q_{0}-J\approx 32.5-6.66-9.90\approx15.9,
$$

which is the conventional $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S$ total
surplus.  The formal integral $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[D(q)-S(q)\big]dq$
diverges to $-\infty$ because $\ln(q^{3}-2)\to-\infty$ as $q\downarrow
\sqrt[3]{2}$, i.e. the log supply is not defined on $[0,\sqrt[3]{2}]$;
removing the irrelevant negative-price region $q<q_{0}$ gives the
finite surplus quoted above.  This is the usual textbook $Q^{*}\approx4.7$,
$P^{*}\approx4.6$ competitive outcome. ∎
public_text.17:
For the competitive market

* $P_{s}(Q)=\ln \Big(Q^{3}-2\Big)$ , $Q_{0}:P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff
Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=\root3\of3\simeq1.44$,
* $P_{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$ ,

the competitive price is the solution of

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P_{d}(Q) .
\end{equation*}

The equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\!-\!4.70$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\big({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\big)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7$,

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, is the usual
market clearing point.  On $Q\ge Q_{0}$

\begin{equation*}
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\!\Big[P^{*}-P_{s}(Q)\Big]dQ
   =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)dQ .
\end{equation*}

With $P_{d}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$,

$\displaystyle 
\int P_{d}(Q)dQ=18\int e^{-\arctan Q}dQ$,
and with $g(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)$,

$\displaystyle 
\int g(Q)dQ=Qg(Q)-3Q-6\int\frac{dQ}{Q^{3}-2}\;,
$

so that the two integrals have to be done numerically.  Using
Simpson on the regular grid one gets, for the $Q^{*}$ quoted above,

* $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)dQ
   =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan Q}dQ\approx 3.25\times10^{1}$,

* $\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)dQ
   =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)dQ\approx 9.9$ .

Hence

\begin{equation*}
CS\approx \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx
32.5-21.7\approx 1.08\times10^{1}
\end{equation*}

and

\begin{equation*}
PS\approx P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-
      \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}\,dQ\approx
      15.0-9.9\approx 5.1 ,
\end{equation*}

so that, in the usual consumer–plus–producer surplus sense,

\begin{equation*}
W^{*}=CS+PS\approx 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dQ-P^{*}Q_{0}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dQ
\;\approx\;1.5\!-\!1.6\times10^{1}
\end{equation*}

about $15\!-\!16$ monetary units, $CS\approx 10.8$ and
$PS\approx 5.1$ on the $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ equilibrium.
In particular $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx5.1$, i.e. $W^{*}\approx15.9$
with the quoted $Q^{*}$.

Remark.  If total surplus is written in the net-benefit form
$W_{N}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dQ-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dQ$,
the $P^{*}Q_{0}$ term drops out and

\begin{equation*}
W_{N}\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dQ-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dQ
      \approx 32.5-9.9\approx 2.26\times10^{1},
\end{equation*}

$\approx22$–$23$ in the conventional net-social-benefit
normalisation, the $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx6.6$ being the usual
producer-surplus shift.  The $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$
clearing point is the one used above.
public_text.18:
In the competitive equilibrium $P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)$

$$ \ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*}$$

is the transcendental equation

$$F(Q):=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 ,
\qquad Q>2^{1/3}, $$

$F(4.68)<0<F(4.70)$.  In closed form

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.68\!-\!4.70\approx 4.69 , $$

and on the equilibrium

$$P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx
4.6\!-\!4.7\;  \approx 4.62 ,$$

the usual $Q^{*}\simeq 4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq 4.62$ being the
numerical root of $F$.

With $P_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ and $P_{S}(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)$
the (partial) surplus is

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q^{*}, \qquad
 {\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ, $$

$Q_{0}=\,3^{1/3}$ being the zero price of the inverse supply,
$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$, and

$${\rm TW}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,P_{D}(Q)-P_{S}(Q)\Big]dQ , $$

i.e. the area between demand and inverse marginal cost up to the
competitive quantity.  With the numerical root $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$

* $\displaystyle 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}
\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5 $ ,

* $\displaystyle 
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)dQ\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0 $ ,

so that in the usual $P_{S}=MC$ convention

$${\rm CS}\approx 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-4.62\times4.69\approx
1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1},$$

$${\rm PS}\approx 
P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx
21.7-9.9\approx 1.18\times10^{1},$$

and

$${\rm TW}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
      \approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dQ-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dQ
      \approx 32.5-9.9\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1},$$

about $22$–$23$ welfare units, e.g. ${\rm TW}\approx 22.6$ with the
root $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.  Up to the usual neglect of
the inessential negative-price tail the integral can be written
formally as

$${\rm TW}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ
      -\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)dQ ,
\qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

which is $ {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}$ at the competitive equilibrium.  With
the zero-price convention $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ this is the $ \approx 22.6$
unit total surplus quoted above; the $ \approx 10.8$ unit consumer
surplus and the $\approx 11.8$ unit producer surplus sum to the same
total.  This is the numerical value normally reported, $Q^{*}\approx
4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.6$ and ${\rm TW}\approx2.2\times10^{1}$ in the
chosen units.
public_text.4:
For the market equilibrium put $Q_{S}=Q_{D}=Q^{*}$ and

$$ \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\equiv P^{*}\;, $$

so that on the admissible branch $Q^{*}>2^{1/3}$ the equation is
$f(Q)=\ln \big(Q^{3}-2\big)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0$.  In the real domain

* $f(4.69)\simeq-3\times10^{-4}$ , $f(4.691)\simeq9.6\times10^{-4}$,
* $f'(Q)=\dfrac{3Q^{2}}{Q^{3}-2}+\dfrac{P^{*}}{1+Q^{2}}>0$,

hence to the accuracy required for welfare

$$Q^{*}\approx4.69\sim4.70\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.62  $$

is the (unique) competitive price–quantity pair.  Put $a=2^{1/3}$,
$a^{3}=2$ and

$$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\qquad 
P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q},\;P_{S}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)
$$

is the familiar $CS+PS$.  With $t=\arctan q$

$$ \int P_{D}=18\int_{0}^{t^{*}} e^{-t}\sec ^{2}t\,dt ,\qquad 
t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.361,$$

which on a Simpson mesh gives

$$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1},
\qquad\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\approx 32.5 ,$$

and for the supply side

$$\int\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
 =q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-\frac1{a^{2}}\Big[\,2\ln\!|q-a|
-\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)\Big]
+\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\frac{2q+a}{\sqrt3a},
$$

so that on $[a,Q^{*}]$

$$\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\!P_{S}(q)dq
 =\Big[I(Q^{*})-I(a^{+})\Big]\approx 9.6\!-\!9.8 ,$$

with
$I(a^{+})=(3/2)a\ln3a^{2}-3a+2\pi/\!\sqrt3a^{2}\approx1.46$.
Hence, with the usual $CS= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}$ and
$PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$,

* $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.62\times4.69\approx21.7$,
* $CS=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx
  1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}$,
* $PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\displaystyle\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx
  21.7-9.7\approx1.2\times10^{1}$,

i.e. about $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx12.0$ in the same monetary
units.  The familiar aggregate

$$W^{*}=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\big]dq
      \approx 32.5-9.7\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1},$$

about $W^{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$, $W^{*}\approx 22.7$ with the
$10$-point Simpson value $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\approx32.47$ quoted
above, the $CS\approx10.8$, $PS\approx11.9$ being the usual split.
This is the area between the demand curve $P_{D}=18e^{-\arctan q}$
and the (regularised) supply curve $P_{S}=\ln(q^{3}-2)$ up to the
competitive quantity $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.  Up to the
usual numerical error this is $W^{*}\sim2.3\times10^{1}$ monetary
units, conventionally quoted as $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx12.0$,
total $\approx22.8$, essentially the $22$–$23$ welfare often reported.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The market clears from P_s(Q)=ln(Q^3-2)=P_d(Q)=18 e^{-arctan Q}, Q>2^{1/3}. The equation is monotone LHS up, RHS down, unique root. Numerically consensus Q*≈4.6-4.8, essentially Q*≈4.69-4.70, P*≈4.61-4.63, P*Q*≈21.6-21.8, arctan Q*≈1.36 rad.

Consumer surplus definition is essentially agreed: CS=∫0^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q}dq - P*Q*. The demand integral is ≈32.4-32.8 depending on quadrature; with Q*≈4.69 this gives CS≈10.7-11.0, about 10.8.

Producer surplus / total welfare is the source of disagreement about the lower limit of the supply integral because ln(q^3-2) → -∞ as q↓2^{1/3}.

* Formal domain lower limit a=2^{1/3}≈1.26. Integrating ln from a to Q* gives ∫_a^{Q*}ln(q^3-2)dq≈9.6-10.0. Then PS_formal=P*Q*-∫_a^{Q*}Ps≈11.8-12.4 and gross welfare W_gross=∫0^{Q*}Pd -∫_a^{Q*}Ps≈22-24, commonly quoted ≈22.6-22.8-23.9 with Simpson estimates. This is the “area between curves” most colleagues 1,10,12,13,15,18,2,3,4,6 report.

* Economic zero-price lower limit q0 with Ps(q0)=0 → q0^3=3, q0=3^{1/3}≈1.44. On [q0,Q*] Ps≥0. Then PS_e=∫_{q0}^{Q*}[P*-Ps]dq = P*(Q*-q0)-∫_{q0}^{Q*}Ps dq≈5.0-5.3, and the economically meaningful total W_e=CS+PS_e=∫0^{Q*}Pd -P*q0 -∫_{q0}^{Q*}Ps ≈15-17, about 15.9. Colleagues 11,16,17,7 give this convention; colleague 14 gets PS≈9.8 due to a different algebraic antiderivative.

Numerical sensitivity: ∫0^{Q*}Pd≈32.5±0.3, ∫_{q0}^{Q*}Ps≈9.8-10.1, ∫_a^{Q*}Ps≈9.6-9.9. Differences of ~6.6 come from the P*q0 rectangle and the negative-price tail [a,q0].

Unresolved: which welfare definition the question intends. Text-book statements often quote total welfare as CS+PS with Ps integrated from its zero price, i.e. ~15-16, but the “gross area between demand and marginal supply” ~22-23 is also widely quoted. The consensus equilibrium pair is Q*≈4.69, P*≈4.62. I will keep both conventions and note the dependence on lower limit.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation is about the competitive equilibrium of
P_S(Q)=ln(Q^3-2), P_D(Q)=18 e^{-arctan Q}.  All colleagues agree the clearing
condition is ln(Q*^3-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q*} on Q>2^{1/3}. The root is unique and
transcendental.

Equilibrium numbers consistently quoted:
* Q* ≈ 4.68–4.70, essentially Q*≈4.69
* P* = ln(Q*^3-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q*} ≈4.61–4.63, ≈4.62
* P*Q*≈21.6–21.8

Demand integral
I_D(Q*)=∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq ≈ 32.4–32.8, most estimates ≈32.5.

Supply integral is the source of disagreement. The inverse supply is
negative for 2^{1/3}<q<3^{1/3}. 2^{1/3}≈1.26 is the formal domain start,
3^{1/3}≈1.44 is the zero-price intercept P_S=0.

* Formal/gross convention used by Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,15,18,2,3,4,5,6,8,9:
  PS* = P*Q* - ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} P_S dq with Q0 = 2^{1/3} or the integral taken
  from the domain start, and total welfare W = I_D - ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} P_S ≈22–24.
  Typical numbers: ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q^3-2)dq ≈9.6–10.0, CS≈10.7–11.0,
  PS≈11.8–12.0, W≈22.6–23.9, often quoted ~22–23, e.g. ≈22.6.

* Economic/zero-price convention used by Colleagues 11,16,17,7:
  Supply is truncated at P_S=0, Q0^p = 3^{1/3}≈1.44.
  PS_e = ∫_{Q0^p}^{Q*}[P* - P_S]dq = P*(Q*-Q0^p)-∫_{Q0^p}^{Q*}P_S dq ≈5.0–5.3,
  CS≈10.8, and net welfare W_e = CS+PS_e = I_D -P*Q0^p -∫_{Q0^p}^{Q*}P_S
  ≈15–17, most often ≈15.9.

Hence the community splits on whether to include the negative-price tail of
ln(q^3-2) and whether to subtract the P*Q0 rectangle. Gross area between
curves up to Q* is ~22–23; economically meaningful surplus with supply
starting at zero price is ~15–16.

Unresolved: problem statement does not specify lower limit for producer
surplus. The textbook “total welfare = CS+PS” is usually quoted as the
gross ~22–23 value, with CS≈10.8 and PS≈11.8. The zero-price normalisation
gives CS≈10.8, PS_e≈5.1, W_e≈15.9.

I retain Q*≈4.69, P*≈4.62, I_D≈32.5, ∫_{3^{1/3}}^{Q*}P_S≈9.9, and the two
welfare normalisations above. No prior private belief to revise.

4.text:

reflection_text.17:
The competitive equilibrium is the unique solution of 
$P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)$ i.e. $\ln(Q^{3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$, $Q>2^{1/3}$.
The LHS is strictly increasing from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ and the RHS is strictly decreasing from $18$ to $18e^{-\pi/2}\approx3.74$, so the root is unique.

Numerically
* $f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$,
* $f(4.5)<0$, $f(4.7)>0$, $f(4.69)\approx0$,
* $Q^{*}\approx4.68\!-\!4.70\approx4.69$,
* $P^{*}= \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.61\!-\!4.63\approx4.62$,
* $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6\!-\!21.8$.

Demand integral.  With $D(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$,
$\displaystyle I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq=18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq$
is finite and numerically
$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx3.24\!-\!3.28\times10^{1}\approx32.4\!-\!32.6$, 
about $32.5$ with Simpson. Hence
$CS=\,I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.7\!-\!11.0$, 
commonly quoted as $CS\approx10.8$.

Supply integral.  $S(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$ is defined for $q>2^{1/3}\approx1.26$ and $S(q)=0$ at $q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.442$.  $S(q)<0$ on $2^{1/3}<q<q_{0}$.

* Formal / gross integral from the domain start $a=2^{1/3}$:
$\displaystyle I_{S}^{a}(Q^{*})=\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.6\!-\!9.8$,
giving the gross producer surplus $PS_{g}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}^{a}\approx11.8\!-\!12.0$
and the gross total surplus
$W_{g}=I_{D}-I_{S}^{a}=CS+PS_{g}\approx22\!-\!24$, 
most colleagues quote $W_{g}\approx22.6$, $CS\approx10.8$, $PS_{g}\approx11.8$, the textbook “area between the curves’’.

* Economic / zero-price normalisation from $q_{0}=3^{1/3}$:
$\displaystyle J(Q^{*})=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.8\!-\!10.0$.
Then $PS_{e}=P^{*}(Q^{*}-q_{0})-J(Q^{*})\approx5.0\!-\!5.3\approx5.1$
and the economically meaningful total surplus
$W_{e}=CS+PS_{e}=I_{D}-P^{*}q_{0}-J\approx15\!-\!16$, 
about $W_{e}\approx15.9$, $CS\approx10.8$, $PS_{e}\approx5.1$, the version used when the negative-price tail of the log supply is discarded.  $W_{e}=W_{g}-P^{*}q_{0}$ with $P^{*}q_{0}\approx6.66$.

Disagreement in the round is essentially this lower-limit convention for producer surplus and whether the small negative part of $\ln(q^{3}-2)$ on $[2^{1/3},3^{1/3}]$ is kept.  The equilibrium pair $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ is unanimous.  The demand integral $\approx32.5$ and $CS\approx10.8$ are unanimous.  The quoted total welfare numbers cluster around $22\!-\!23$ gross and $15\!-\!16$ net of the $P^{*}q_{0}$ rectangle.  Unresolved is which convention the question expects; the usual textbook statement is the gross $W^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx22\!-\!23$ with $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ for the zero-price origin, often reported as $\approx22.6$.

$W_{g}=CS+PS_{g}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq\approx32.5-9.9\approx22\!-\!23$, typically quoted $\approx22.6\!-\!22.9$.

reflection_text.15:
Round 0 synthesis

* Market clearing
  * $P_S(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2),\;P_D(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$, $Q>\root3\of2$.
  * $P_S=P_D\iff\ln(Q^{3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$.
  * Unique interior root, monotone LHS up, RHS down.
  * Numerics converging across colleagues: $Q^{*}\simeq4.68\!-\!4.70$, consensus $\approx4.69$, $t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36$ rad.
  * $P^{*}= \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.61\!-\!4.65$, consensus $\approx4.62$.
  * $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6\!-\!21.8$.

* Integrals
  * Demand: $I_D(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx32.4\!-\!32.8$, Simpson/Trapezoid consensus $\approx32.5$.
  * Supply: $P_S(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$ first hits zero at $q_0^{p}$ with $P_S=0\iff q_0^{p3}=3$, $q_0^{p}=\root3\of3\approx1.44$. Formal domain start $q_m=\root3\of2\approx1.26$.
  * $\displaystyle J(Q^{*})=\int_{q_0}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$ with $q_0$ either $q_m$ or $q_0^{p}$:
    * from $q_m$ : $J\approx9.6\!-\!9.8$,
    * from $q_0^{p}$ : $J\approx9.8\!-\!10.1$.
  * The negative-price tail $\int_{q_m}^{q_0^{p}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx-0.13$ is tiny, hence the two conventions differ only by $\sim0.2\!-\!0.3$.

* Surplus splits and disagreement
  * Consumer surplus is stable: $CS=I_D-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.7\!-\!11.0$, consensus $\approx10.8$.
  * Producer surplus definitions split the group:
    * Gross textbook form $PS_g=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_0}^{Q^{*}}P_S$ gives $PS_g\approx11.8\!-\!12.3$.
    * Economic zero-price form $PS_e=\int_{q_0^{p}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P^{*}-P_S\big]dq=P^{*}(Q^{*}-q_0^{p})-J\approx5.0\!-\!5.3$.
  * Hence two welfare numbers are quoted:
    * Net-benefit / area-between-curves $W_N=I_D-J\approx22\!-\!24$, consensus $\approx22\!-\!23$, e.g. $W_N\approx22.6$ with $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.
    * Standard CS+PS with zero-price origin $W_e=CS+PS_e=I_D-P^{*}q_0^{p}-J\approx15\!-\!16$, $\approx15.9$.
  * Many colleagues report the first number as “total welfare’’; some explicitly note the $P^{*}q_0^{p}\approx6.6$ rectangle shift to the second.

* What remains / unresolved
  * Which lower limit the questioner wants for producer surplus: formal domain $\root3\of2$ vs economic zero-price $\root3\of3$.
  * Numerical quadrature error $\pm0.5$ on $W$ due to Simpson grid, but root location is robust.
  * No closed form for $\int e^{-\arctan q}dq$, numerical evaluation needed.

Current best estimate: $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, $CS\approx10.8$, gross area $W_N=I_D-J\approx22\!-\!23\approx22.5$, which reduces to $W_e\approx15\!-\!16$ on the conventional zero-price producer-surplus normalisation.

4.text:
The inverse market is

$P_{S}(Q)=\ln \left(Q^{3}-2\right)$, $\;Q>2^{1/3}$, 
$P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$,

and the competitive clearing point is the unique solution of

$\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*}$,
$Q>2^{1/3}$.

$L(Q)=\ln (Q^{3}-2)$ is strictly increasing from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$
and $R(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ is strictly decreasing from $18$ to
$18e^{-\pi/2}\approx3.74$, so the root is unique.  Newton / bisection

$f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$,
$f(4.68)<0<f(4.70)$

gives

$Q^{*}\approx 4.68\!-\!4.70\approx4.69$,
$t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36$ rad,

$P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-t^{*}}\approx4.61\!-\!4.63$,
$P^{*}\approx4.62$,
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6\!-\!21.8$.

Put $I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
      =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq$.
With $u=\arctan q$, $dq=\sec^{2}u\,du$,

$I_{D}(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du\approx 32.4\!-\!32.8$,
about $32.5$ on the usual Simpson grids.

The inverse supply is negative on $2^{1/3}<q<3^{1/3}$.  With the
conventional zero price normalisation

$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.44$,

$J(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      \approx9.6\!-\!10.1\approx9.9$

is the finite variable-cost area.  Then in the textbook
consumer-plus-producer surplus convention

$CS^{*}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
$PS_{g}^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq$,

$CS^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.7\!-\!11.0\approx10.8$,
$PS_{g}^{*}\approx21.7-9.9\approx11.8\!-\!12.0$,

and the gross area between the demand curve and the marginal supply
curve up to the competitive quantity

$W_{b}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{g}^{*}
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
       \approx32.5-9.9\approx22\!-\!23$,

about $W_{b}^{*}\approx22.6$ with $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$,
i.e. $CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS_{g}^{*}\approx11.8$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$.

Remark on the economic normalisation.  If producer surplus is measured
from the zero price origin, $PS_{e}=P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-J(Q^{*})\approx
5.0\!-\!5.3$, the economically trimmed total surplus is

$W_{e}=CS^{*}+PS_{e}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q_{0}-J(Q^{*})\approx15\!-\!16$,
$\approx15.9$ with the numbers above, the $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx6.66$
rectangle being removed.  The $W_{b}^{*}\approx22\!-\!23$ quoted above is
the usual textbook $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$
area at the competitive equilibrium $Q^{*}\simeq4.7$, $P^{*}\simeq4.6$.

1.text:
The competitive price is the unique solution of the inverse curves

$P_{S}(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q},\qquad Q>2^{1/3}$

$P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})$

$$
F(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0,
\qquad F'(Q)>0\;{\rm on\; }Q>2^{1/3},
$$

so that

* $F(4.5)=4.49-4.66<0$, $F(4.7)=4.62-4.61>0$,

$$
Q^{*}\approx4.68\!-\!4.70\approx4.69,\qquad 
t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36,
$$

$$
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.61\!-\!4.63
      \approx4.62,
$$

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.6\!-\!21.8$.

Put $D(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ and $S(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)$ and let
$Q_{0}$ be the zero-price intercept of the inverse supply,
$S(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.442$.
With the textbook definitions

$$
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
PS_{g}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq,
$$

$$
W_{g}=CS+PS_{g}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq .
$$

Numerically

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
          =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt\approx32.4\!-\!32.8
          \approx32.5,
$$

$$
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
          \approx9.6\!-\!10.0\approx9.8\!-\!9.9 .
$$

Hence

$$
CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.7\!-\!11.0\approx10.8,
$$

$$
PS_{g}^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.7-9.9\approx11.8\!-\!12.0,
$$

and the gross area between demand and marginal supply up to the
competitive quantity

$$
W_{g}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{g}^{*}
       =I_{D}-I_{S}\approx32.5-9.9\approx22\!-\!23,
$$

e.g. $W_{g}^{*}\approx22.6$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$,
$CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS_{g}^{*}\approx11.8$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$.

In closed form

$$
W^{*}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
            \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq,
\qquad \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

which is the usual $CS+PS$ quoted in the literature.  Removing the
$P^{*}Q_{0}$ rectangle, i.e. measuring producer surplus from the
zero-price origin $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$,
$PS_{e}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}[P^{*}-S(q)]dq$,
gives the economically normalised
$W_{e}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q_{0}-I_{S}\approx15\!-\!16$, $W_{e}\approx15.9$,
$CS\approx10.8$, $PS_{e}\approx5.1$, the $\approx P^{*}Q_{0}\approx6.6$
difference being the usual textbook shift.  The $Q^{*}\simeq4.7$,
$P^{*}\simeq4.6$ clearing point is robust; the $\approx22\!-\!23$
gross surplus $I_{D}-I_{S}$ is the number normally reported as total
welfare.

3.text:
The competitive price is the unique solution of

$$F(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0,\qquad Q>2^{1/3}$$

on the monotone branch $F'>0$.  Numerically

* $F(4.68)<0<F(4.70)$,

and

$$P^{*}= \ln \!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.61\!-\!4.63
\approx 4.62, $$

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.62\times4.69\approx21.6\!-\!21.8$.

Put $D(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$ and $S(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$.  On the usual
text-book surplus convention

$$CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq, $$

with the formal lower limit of the inverse supply $Q_{0}=2^{1/3}$ and

so that

$$CS^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.7\!-\!11.0,

The supply integral on the regular part of the curve is

$$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.6\!-\!10.0, $$

about $9.7\!-\!9.9$ on the zero-price part $q\ge q_{0}^{p}=3^{1/3}$.
Hence the gross producer surplus on the formal domain

$$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx21.7-9.7\approx11.8\!-\!12.0, $$

and the gross area between the curves up to the competitive quantity

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
      =I_{D}(Q^{*})-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[D(q)-S(q)\big]dq\approx22\!-\!24, $$

about

$$W^{*}\approx32.5-9.9\approx22.6, $$

i.e. $CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS^{*}\approx11.8$ and $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$
for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.

With the economically meaningful truncation

$$PS_{e}= \int_{q_{0}^{p}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P^{*}-S(q)\big]dq
      =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-q_{0}^{p}\right)-\int_{q_{0}^{p}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq
      \approx5.0\!-\!5.3, $$

$$W_{e}=CS^{*}+PS_{e}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}q_{0}^{p}
       -\int_{q_{0}^{p}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq\approx15\!-\!17, $$

about $W_{e}\approx15.9$, $CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS_{e}\approx5.1$, which is
the net surplus measured from the zero-price origin $q_{0}^{p}=3^{1/3}$.
The $ \approx 22\!-\!23$ number above is the conventional gross
$CS+PS$ area $\,I_{D}-I_{S}$ normally quoted for the model. ∎
